proposed_edges.relationship: Native Canadians 'cannot enjoy fully "post-coloniality"'; a postcolonial reader that represents Natives 'only through non-Native Canadians' is 'unacceptable' (1999); the charge recurs in the 2010 book
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 50–51 (read 2026-10-28): in The Post-Colonial Studies Reader 'no Native writers or scholars are included … I find it unacceptable in a postcolonial reader, especially one published in the 1990s, that Natives are represented only through non-Native Canadians'; 'Obviously, Native Canadians cannot enjoy fully "post-coloniality" since their colonial experience is imbricated with the past and present.' PDF p. 40: in Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin 'it is the re/settler whites who are treated as the colonized resisting the mother country'. PDF p. 70: she will avoid the 'obscure language which has become such an uncontrollable part of post-colonial criticism'. 2010 book, p. 167, as quoted by Black (AICRJ 2011, p. 285, read in full): 'some scholars live in the illusion that … by their postcolonial powers of analysis, they have neutralized the colonial experience'. A critique of the field's scope and practice; she also uses its resources (Said, edge_2140). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Finds Sioui's call for 'an ethical approach to history' appealing but his autohistory 'at times obscure' on historical method, and his 'ideological portrait of Amerindians' too close to the Noble Savage (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 240–241 (read 2026-10-28): 'Sioui's thesis on "autohistory" is at times obscure, especially when he turns to the issue of historical methodology'; it is 'not at all clear whether he is espousing a "division of labour" between white and Native (or Huron?) historians'; 'Parts of Sioui's proposal … is appealing, for example, his call for "an ethical approach to history"'; 'I have difficulty with his idealization … to the extent the portrait resembles the Noble Savage.' A qualified critique, distinct from her critique of Trigger's foreword to the same book (edge_2166). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Takes Fanon and Memmi as 'the classic sources' on internalised colonisation, while noting that The Wretched of the Earth does not treat Native North Americans (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 48, 'Frantz Fanon and Albert Memmi are the classic sources for discussion on the processes of internalization'; PDF p. 12, classic (Fanon, Memmi) and contemporary works 'have convincingly shown that colonization produces a pervasive structural and psychological relationship between the colonizer and the colonized'; PDF p. 40 (qualification), 'Frantz Fanon in Wretched of the Earth does not deal with the treatment of Native North Americans either'. Parallel to edge_2140 (Said). Memmi has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Reads Mandelbaum's The Plains Cree (1940) as dividing Cree technology 'into disparate pieces, giving the impression of a people frozen in time', a book taught without discussion of its 'Eurocentric assumptions' (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 107–108 (read 2026-10-28), after Duchemin on Mackenzie's 'ethnographical curiosities': 'This is very similar to my reading of David Mandelbaum's treatment of Cree "tools" in The Plains Cree. Mandelbaum, one of the earlier anthropologists in the 1930s to study the Plains Cree, divides Cree technology into disparate pieces, giving the impression of a people frozen in time'; 'This book was first published in 1940 but I do not recall any discussion about its Eurocentric assumptions.' Her personal recollections on p. 108 are not used. Black (AICRJ 2011, p. 286) lists 'anthropologists (David Mandelbaum)' among the colonial authors treated in the 2010 book. Mandelbaum has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Charges fur-trade historians with a 'double standard': Indians generalised as of 'covetous disposition' while European self-interest is overlooked; E. E. Rich 'persistently uses colonial phrases' such as 'crafty' and 'shrewd enough' (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 102, 'It is quite common, for example, for fur trade historians to generalize Indians as having a "covetous disposition," quite obviously employing the double standard by over-looking European self-interests'; PDF p. 109, 'fur trade historian E.E. Rich persistently uses colonial phrases such as "crafty," "shrewd enough," "sophisticated enough" or "hardened enough" when describing Indians taking advantage of competition'; 'Even the more objective John C. Ewers qualifies his compliments'; she cites Walker (1971, p. 34) as noticing the same contradiction. The existing native_newcomer roster row already cites pp. 102, 109. Rich has no node or roster row; the strand holds the fur trade as national economic history. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Counts Dickason's The Myth of the Savage, by 'the prolific pace-setting scholar', among Native counter-works on the Indian image: 'clearly anti-colonial' (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 190, works 'range from my slim Defeathering The Indian … to the voluminous The Myth of the Savage by the prolific pace-setting scholar Olive Patricia Dickason. Such productions have not been well understood as the resistance works that they in fact are'; PDF p. 191, the title 'represents more closely Western rather than Native tradition. Still, I consider it an expression of resistance for it is clearly anti-colonial.' PDF p. 21: she moves away from what Dickason calls 'that strain of tolerance toward Amerindians' in European thought, a qualified use. A reading and alignment, not a claim of personal debt. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

new_sources.title: Jason Edward Black, review of Emma LaRocque, When the Other Is Me: Native Resistance Discourse, 1850–1990, American Indian Culture and Research Journal 35:4 (2011): 285–288.
new_sources.citation: Jason Edward Black, review of Emma LaRocque, When the Other Is Me: Native Resistance Discourse, 1850–1990 (Winnipeg: University of Manitoba Press, 2010), American Indian Culture and Research Journal 35, no. 4 (2011): 285–288.

verification.note: Read in full (open access, CC BY-NC, eScholarship). Header gives 'Winnipeg: University of Manitoba Press, 2010' (p. 285). Black places the book's framework in 'decolonial theory (particularly in Native studies and postcolonial studies literature)' (p. 285); quotes LaRocque, p. 167: 'some scholars live in the illusion that they not only understand "Natives," but that somehow, by their postcolonial powers of analysis, they have neutralized the colonial experience' (p. 285); lists 'anthropologists (David Mandelbaum)' among the colonial authors treated in chs. 2–3 (p. 286). The book itself is unread.
